title: A federal procurement chief, Thrive Capital and sole-source awards
summary: Documented: Josh Gruenbaum, as GSA's FAS commissioner, arranged early meetings with Thrive- and Founders Fund-backed Ramp over a SmartPay pilot of up to $25M, prompting Rep. Connolly's May 2025 letter. FAS's TTS gave Thrive-led Databricks a sole-source order with a $1.824M ceiling in Feb 2026, not $18M. Gruenbaum's own $100,001-$250,000 stake, reportedly in a Databricks-linked Thrive SPV, and the claim that GSA's administrator blocked a Ramp award and pushed him out rest on a single WSJ report seen only via aggregators. He says he disclosed, got ethics approval and recused himself, and Thrive denies discussing contracts. The family layer is that he simultaneously worked for Jared Kushner on Gaza and the Board of Peace; a Thrive stake in OneGov vendor Anthropic is unverified.

sub_claims.statement: GSA's Federal Acquisition Service commissioner Josh Gruenbaum (ex-KKR, ex-Moelis) helped arrange early meetings between GSA and Ramp, a startup backed by Thrive and Founders Fund, about a SmartPay charge-card pilot worth up to $25M.
sub_claims.finding: DOCUMENTED. ProPublica (2025-04-17) reported that senior GSA officials met Ramp executives at least four times before a public SmartPay opportunity opened (a Commercial Solutions Opening, RFI issued 2025-03-20), and that Gruenbaum organized some of the meetings. The pilot was worth up to $25M within SmartPay, which the coverage calls a roughly $700B program. Ramp's first and largest investor is Peter Thiel's Founders Fund (seven rounds). Thrive participated in Ramp's June 2025 Series E and later rounds, and per Bloomberg sources co-led a reported ~$1.85B round at about $60B in Oct 2026 (Ramp has not confirmed). GSA rejected any suggestion of preferential contracting. Gruenbaum had been at KKR for almost five years (director, credit team) and earlier at Moelis. What this does not show: no source says Ramp was ever awarded the pilot.

sub_claims.statement: Rep. Gerald Connolly opened a congressional probe of the Ramp courtship.
sub_claims.finding: DOCUMENTED. On 2025-05-09 Connolly, then Oversight ranking member, wrote to Acting GSA Administrator Stephen Ehikian. He asked for Ramp's bids, the RFI timeline and communications with officials tied to the President and DOGE, with a reply due 2025-05-23 (Oversight Democrats release and letter PDF; Banking Dive). Connolly died on 2025-05-21, and we found no public GSA response or follow-up finding. 2026 aggregator write-ups that describe Connolly as 'probing' the Thrive investment repeat the 2025 letter: the letter predates the WSJ disclosure by about a year and does not mention Thrive or Gruenbaum's investment.

sub_claims.statement: Gruenbaum personally invested $100,001-$250,000 in a Thrive Capital vehicle in March 2025.
sub_claims.finding: SINGLE-SOURCE (WSJ, late May 2026, seen only through aggregators: Crypto Briefing 2026-05-31, Edgen in several languages, EconoTimes, and Wikipedia). The WSJ itself could not be reached. As relayed, Gruenbaum put $100,001-$250,000 (an OGE disclosure value band) through a private wealth manager into a special-purpose vehicle tied to Databricks, described as a $194M Thrive vehicle. Gruenbaum says he disclosed it, got ethics approval and recused himself from the matters; he provided documentation to the WSJ. Some senior GSA officials reportedly did not know about it. We could not see his OGE 278 form. Rated unverified only because it rests on one outlet seen secondhand; the WSJ is credible and nobody denies the investment itself. Audit: the WSJ's own Threads post ('Disclosure documents show Josh Gruenbaum was an investor in a Thrive Capital fund while the firm's portfolio companies were up for contracts') and an Investing.com relay ('DOGE official discussed contracts tied to firm he invested in, WSJ reports') confirm that the WSJ published the story; the investment is still one outlet's reporting. A GSA official told the WSJ that Gruenbaum recused himself and did not advocate for Ramp specifically; a contracting-news summary (samsearch/Govly, single-source) adds that he was subject to an internal GSA review of his Ramp communications in Feb 2026.

sub_claims.statement: GSA later awarded Thrive-backed Databricks a sole-source contract.
sub_claims.finding: DOCUMENTED for the award (contract records); the link to the investment is single-source. GSA's Technology Transformation Service (part of FAS, which Gruenbaum ran) posted a sole-source justification on 2026-02-10 for 'Databricks Engineering Services' (order 47QPCA26F0011 under MAS contract 47QTCA25D00D3), citing FAR 8.401(b) and GSAR 538.7104-3(b)(3). The order is fixed-price, five months, with a ceiling of $1,824,000 (HigherGov). That settles the aggregators' '$18M' figure as an error; the WSJ figure is $1.8M. Thrive led Databricks's $10B Series J in Dec 2024 at a $62B valuation (Gunderson Dettmer, Alternatives Watch). Per the WSJ as relayed, the award came about ten months after the investment, and Gruenbaum says he recused himself. What this does not show: no source says Gruenbaum signed or steered this order, and a $1.8M software-services order is immaterial to a ~$100B+ company. The issue is the appearance of a conflict and whether the recusal was effective. Audit: HigherGov, govcontractfinder and samsearch mirrors again show Databricks Federal LLC, order 47QPCA26F0011, ceiling $1,824,000, five months, one bidder, posted 10 Feb 2026 by TTS.

sub_claims.statement: GSA's administrator blocked a Ramp award in April 2026 and asked Gruenbaum to step aside; he then left FAS.
sub_claims.finding: DEPARTURE DOCUMENTED; THE REASON IS SINGLE-SOURCE. Federal News Network first reported in April 2026 that Gruenbaum was leaving FAS, and Nextgov, Washington Technology and MeriTalk followed. GSA Administrator Ed Forst named Laura Stanton acting commissioner. SINGLE-SOURCE (WSJ via Edgen; people familiar): Forst blocked a ~$25M Ramp award in April and asked Gruenbaum to go. Gruenbaum says his departure was planned and voluntary. Timing tension we could not resolve: an aggregator copy of SAM.gov shows GSA cancelled the commercial-payments CSO (47QRAB25R0002) on 2026-02-11, citing a shift to next-generation SmartPay. So either the Ramp award was a different vehicle, or the 'April block' was of something already wound down. GSA named a permanent FAS commissioner, a former banking executive, in Nov 2026.

sub_claims.statement: Thrive and Ramp deny any improper contact.
sub_claims.finding: DOCUMENTED as statements. Thrive: neither Thrive nor Joshua Kushner discussed government contracts with Gruenbaum (WSJ, as relayed). Ramp said it was unaware of the investment (C66). GSA, in 2025, rejected any suggestion of preferential contracting (ProPublica). Gruenbaum says he disclosed, got ethics approval and recused himself. We found no GSA OIG item on the matter in the Oct 2025-Mar 2026 semiannual report.

sub_claims.statement: Gruenbaum, who led GSA's OneGov programme, struck government-wide deals with AI companies in which Thrive holds stakes (OpenAI, Anthropic and others).
sub_claims.finding: DOCUMENTED for OpenAI and Perplexity; UNVERIFIED for Anthropic. GSA's OneGov deals ran through FAS under Gruenbaum. They include OpenAI's ChatGPT Enterprise at $1 per agency (2025-08-06; Gruenbaum quoted in the GSA release urging other AI firms to 'follow OpenAI's lead'), Anthropic's Claude at $1 (2025-08-12), Google Gemini (2025-08), Meta Llama (2025-09) and xAI. Perplexity at $0.25 per agency (2025-11-19) was the first direct-to-government OneGov deal. On 2026-09-10 a follow-on, consumption-based OpenAI deal was signed after he left. Thrive's stakes: OpenAI is documented as a major Thrive holding (C66), and OpenAI took an equity stake in Thrive Holdings on 2025-12-01, about four months after the first OneGov deal. Thrive's Perplexity stake comes from aggregator portfolio tables only (single-source). Anthropic: Anthropic's Series E and F announcements list ICONIQ, Lightspeed, Fidelity and others; one aggregator (F4 Fund) lists Thrive, but no primary source does. We could not confirm a Thrive stake in Anthropic, so that part of the claim is unverified. The $1 deals are near-free and are not shown to have generated revenue for the vendors. No source alleges Gruenbaum's Thrive vehicle held OpenAI or that his recusal covered OneGov. Disclosure: Anthropic, which makes the model that wrote this report, is one of the OneGov companies. It is treated here like every other vendor.

sub_claims.statement: Beyond Josh Kushner: the same official worked directly for Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Gaza diplomacy and the Board of Peace, while holding a Josh Kushner fund investment.
sub_claims.finding: DOCUMENTED for the roles; the overlap is INFERRED. While running FAS, Gruenbaum helped Jared Kushner and Witkoff negotiate the Gaza ceasefire (Jewish Insider, 2026-01; Politico via Raw Story). In Jan 2026 the White House named him and Aryeh Lightstone senior advisers to the Trump-chaired Board of Peace, where Kushner sits on the executive board. Politico later reported him dropped from Russia-Ukraine and Iran work; sources describe Kushner and Witkoff as still his allies. Jewish Insider (2026-06) says he left government but remains an unpaid Board of Peace adviser. INFERRED (no source makes the link): during the period of his reported Thrive vehicle investment (from March 2025), Gruenbaum was also working under Jared Kushner, whose brother runs Thrive. Jared Kushner co-founded and divested Thrive interests in 2017 (C66). No source says Jared had any role in Gruenbaum's investment or in GSA contracts.

sub_claims.statement: After leaving government, Gruenbaum joined Valor Equity Partners, founded by DOGE veteran and Musk ally Antonio Gracias.
sub_claims.finding: SINGLE-SOURCE (the firm's own team page at valorep.com, seen only as a search-result snippet; the site could not be read directly). The snippet says he joined Valor in 2026 as a Managing Director on the investment team, with KKR and Moelis listed as prior roles. Jewish Insider separately reported in June 2026 that he was 'set to join an investment firm' without naming it. Valor's founder Antonio Gracias led DOGE work at the Social Security Administration until 2025-07-01 (NBC, Fortune), and Gruenbaum was himself one of the Musk-linked DOGE officials brought into GSA. Valor is a long-time SpaceX and Tesla investor (Fortune, NBC). INFERRED: a revolving door from a procurement post to a DOGE-linked investor; no source reports any Valor matter before FAS during his tenure.

corrections: Aggregators give the Databricks award as $18M; contract records show a ceiling of $1,824,000 (order 47QPCA26F0011, Feb 2026, five months).
2026 write-ups describe Rep. Connolly as probing the Thrive investment; his only letter was dated 2025-05-09, was about Ramp's courtship, and he died on 2025-05-21, a year before the WSJ disclosure.
The Databricks order was issued by GSA's Technology Transformation Service (within FAS), not FAS acquisition centres directly; the claim does not say Gruenbaum signed it and no source does.
The claim's 'OneGov deals with OpenAI, Anthropic and others in which Thrive holds stakes': Thrive's OpenAI stake is documented, but no primary source shows a Thrive stake in Anthropic.
Ramp's lead investor is Founders Fund (Thiel); Thrive is a participant, though it reportedly co-led a 2026 round.
denials_and_context: Gruenbaum: disclosed the investment, received ethics approval, recused himself from the relevant matters; departure planned and voluntary.
Thrive: neither Thrive nor Joshua Kushner discussed government contracts with Gruenbaum.
Ramp: unaware of the investment (C66). GSA (2025): rejects any suggestion of unfair or preferential contracting.

OneGov deals at $1 or $0.25 per agency generate little or no direct revenue; their value to vendors is market access. Many other vendors without Thrive ties (Google, Meta, xAI, Microsoft, AWS, Snowflake) got similar deals.
A documented relationship is not proof of wrongdoing; no source alleges that the Databricks order was improperly justified or that Jared Kushner had any role.
Disclosure: Anthropic, maker of the model that produced this report, is one of the OneGov vendors. It is treated like every other company here.
GSA official (per WSJ, relayed): Gruenbaum recused himself from the procurement and did not advocate for Ramp's business specifically.
